passage: The airport was roaring with cancelled-flight announcements, and Baljeet and Vikas had been stuck for three hours. When the cab fare home came up, Vikas snapped, "These cab drivers are all cheats." Baljeet was tired too and felt a flash of irritation, but kept the voice light. "Really? Mine this morning waited fifteen minutes at the gate and charged exactly the meter. Did something happen to you?" Vikas rubbed his neck. "One overcharged me last month, near the station." "That's rotten," Baljeet said. "Ever met a good one?" Vikas paused. "My regular driver, actually. He once drove my mother to hospital at night and refused a tip." "So he's not a cheat?" "No. I suppose not."

qa.q: How long had Baljeet and Vikas been stuck at the airport?
qa.a: They had been stuck for three hours.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel at the sweeping remark, and how did Baljeet respond?
qa.a: A flash of irritation, but Baljeet kept the voice light and asked a question instead of attacking.

qa.q: What worked in Baljeet's approach?
qa.a: Sharing a personal example and asking a curious question kept Vikas's dignity safe, so Vikas could recall a good driver.

qa.q: What might Vikas have been feeling on admitting the regular driver was good?
qa.a: A little sheepish and thoughtful, as a real doubt about the sweeping label began to form.

grounding: A young adult hears a sweeping remark and answers with a question and a personal example instead of attacking.

passage: In the Bengaluru office canteen, Charu stirred the tea and sighed. "Fresh graduates today are all lazy. They want the salary and none of the work." A few colleagues nodded. Chaitanya, two years out of college, felt the sting but did not snap. "Do you mean the ones on our team?" Chaitanya asked. "Well..." "Because last week Priya stayed till nine to fix the client's slides, and she didn't put it on any report." Charu looked into the cup. "Priya did do that, didn't she." "She did. What made you think of it?" "A bad intern, years ago," Charu admitted. Next morning Charu asked Priya to help review the client file.

qa.q: Who stayed till nine to fix the client's slides?
qa.a: Priya stayed till nine to fix the client's slides.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel at the remark, and how did Chaitanya respond?
qa.a: Stung but calm; Chaitanya asked a question and gave a real example instead of snapping.

qa.q: What made Charu's stance shift?
qa.a: A concrete example of Priya's work and a kind question, which let Charu remember an old bad experience without being shamed.

qa.q: How might Priya feel about being asked to help review the client file?
qa.a: Recognised and valued for the quiet extra work.

grounding: A young adult hears a sweeping remark about graduates and asks a question and gives a personal example instead of attacking.

passage:
On the flat's balcony one evening, over tea:
Varun: I have to confess something embarrassing.
Lalremsiami: Uh-oh.
Varun: Before I moved here, my relatives warned me about people from your state. They said you all keep to yourselves and don't mix.
Lalremsiami: And then you met me, the loudest person on the floor.
Varun: And the person who lent me a cooker and stayed up helping me with my resume.
Lalremsiami: I still don't know your aunt.
Varun: I told her about you, actually. She wants to meet you at Diwali.
Lalremsiami: Bring her. I'll make her cook something with me.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami lend Varun?
qa.a: Lalremsiami lent Varun a cooker.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about repeating the warning, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed but honest; Varun calls it a confession and follows it with kind examples of Lalremsiami.

qa.q: What did Varun do that let personal contact replace the warning?
qa.a: Varun told the aunt stories about Lalremsiami and arranged a meeting at Diwali.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt hearing the warning?
qa.a: Amused but perhaps a little stung, since the reply teases first; the offer to cook with the aunt shows openness.

grounding: A young adult makes a friendship across a divide they were warned about and tells the stories at home.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Growing up I was told never to go past the canal, because the colony on the other side was "not our kind". I never asked who had said it. At twenty-four I started at a design firm, and my desk-mate was Pranav, who lived in exactly that colony. He brought jaggery sweets on his birthday and drew a map of his lane for me on a napkin. I went one Sunday, and Pranav's mother scolded me for being thin and fed me twice. I came home and told my family about the fish curry and the cricket in the lane. My grandfather said nothing for a moment, then asked, "Is that where the good chai is?" I said yes. He nodded slowly. Sonali

qa.q: What did Pranav draw for Sonali on a napkin?
qa.a: Pranav drew a map of his lane on a napkin.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about the warning, and how did that change?
qa.a: The warning had gone unquestioned, but after the visit Sonali felt welcomed and fed, and the old idea seemed doubtful.

qa.q: What choice by Sonali helped break the old prejudice?
qa.a: Accepting Pranav's invitation and telling the stories at home.

qa.q: How might Sonali's grandfather have felt on hearing about the colony?
qa.a: Surprised and thoughtful, and a little curious; asking about the chai shows the old warning softening.

grounding: A young adult makes real friendships with people from a group they were warned about and tells the stories.

passage: I'm Reena, and I teach Class 4 in a school in Sydney. Samir's mother came for pickup today and Samir switched to Tamil mid-sentence, laughing, then looked around to see who was near and went quiet. In class Samir speaks careful English, and I have noticed a hand hovering before answering. I can't say for sure what is going on inside. Today at story time Samir said the Tamil word for moon, and a classmate asked, "Say it again!" Samir did, twice, smiling shyly. Afterwards Samir's mother told me they read one Tamil book and one English book every evening. Samir's shoulders looked lighter at the gate.

qa.q: Which language did Samir switch to at pickup?
qa.a: Samir switched to Tamil mid-sentence.

qa.q: What might Samir feel when looking around before going quiet, and how sure is Reena?
qa.a: Perhaps self-conscious about using Tamil near classmates, though Reena says there is no way to be sure what goes on inside.

qa.q: How did the classmate's reaction help Samir?
qa.a: Asking Say it again showed curiosity, which let Samir share the Tamil word proudly.

qa.q: What might Samir's mother want for Samir?
qa.a: For Samir to be at ease in both languages, keeping Tamil warmly while learning English, which the two evening books suggest.

grounding: A child of migrants speaks one language at home and another at school and sometimes seems split; warm support helps.

passage:
Monday. At school in Melbourne, Suraj asked what language Abhinav had been speaking to Ajji on the phone. Abhinav went red and said, "Nothing," then felt bad all the way home.
Tuesday. At dinner Abhinav told Amma and Appa it felt like being two different people. Appa said, "You are one person with two languages, like having two kinds of food." Amma hugged Abhinav and promised nobody would ever ask Abhinav to choose.
Friday. Suraj came over. Abhinav taught Suraj to count to five in Kannada, and Suraj taught Abhinav a football chant. They shouted both at the top of their voices, and Abhinav laughed a lot.

qa.q: What did Suraj ask on Monday?
qa.a: Suraj asked what language Abhinav had been speaking to Ajji on the phone.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav say Nothing, and how did Abhinav feel?
qa.a: Embarrassed and split, unsure whether the home language was welcome at school.

qa.q: What support helped Abhinav most?
qa.a: Appa's comparison of two languages to two kinds of food and Amma's promise not to ask for a choice, followed by sharing words with Suraj.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt learning to count in Kannada?
qa.a: Curious and happy, since Suraj traded words in return and had fun.

grounding: A child of migrants feels split between home and school languages and, with warm support, grows at ease in both.

passage: On the bus from school in Toronto, Sami sat beside Yara, quiet. That summer in Chennai, cousins had teased Sami's accent and called Sami the Canada kid, and an auntie had asked why Sami did not know the name of a sweet. Back at school, a classmate had asked, "But where are you really from?" Sami felt like a coat that fit no shoulder. "It's like I'm visiting everywhere," Sami said. Yara, whose family is from Lebanon, nodded. "I get it. My cousins say I'm too Canadian, my teacher says I'm too something else." They both laughed, a little sadly. That night at dinner Sami told the parents everything. Amma said, "Tell us what you miss and what you like. We're still learning too."

qa.q: Where do Sami and Yara ride the bus from?
qa.a: They ride the bus from school in Toronto.

qa.q: What did Sami mean by feeling like a coat that fit no shoulder?
qa.a: Sami felt like an outsider in both places, not fully belonging anywhere.

qa.q: What helped Sami?
qa.a: Talking with Yara, who understood, and then telling the parents openly at dinner.

qa.q: How might Yara see Sami's struggle?
qa.a: With understanding from a similar experience, since Yara's own cousins say Yara is too Canadian.

grounding: A teenager born abroad to Indian parents feels foreign in both places, and a friend with a similar background and open family talk help.

passage: In the school counsellor's room in Birmingham, Vinita twisted a sleeve. "In Delhi last year, everyone said my Hindi sounded like a textbook. Here, someone asked why my lunch smells. I don't feel Indian or English." Manoj, the counsellor, waited a moment and then said, "That sounds lonely." Vinita nodded, eyes stinging. Manoj asked whether Vinita knew others with two homes. "Maybe Priya from the debating club? Her parents are from Kerala." Manoj suggested the school's cultural society and asked whether Vinita would like to talk with the parents about it too. "I'd try the society," Vinita said. At the door Vinita stopped. "Can I come again next week?" "Anytime," said Manoj.

qa.q: Where does Vinita meet Manoj?
qa.a: Vinita meets Manoj in the school counsellor's room in Birmingham.

qa.q: How does Vinita feel about identity, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lonely and in between; Vinita feels neither Indian nor English, and the eyes sting when the counsellor names it.

qa.q: What steps might help Vinita?
qa.a: Joining the cultural society, meeting students who also have two homes, and talking with the parents.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Vinita's question about coming again?
qa.a: As a sign that Vinita feels heard and trusts the counsellor.

grounding: A teenager born abroad to Indian parents feels foreign in both countries and finds support through a counsellor and peers with similar backgrounds.

passage: Twenty minutes before the Diwali party in the community hall in Leicester, rain drummed on the car roof while Irfan waited outside Vaibhav's house. Through the window Irfan heard Vaibhav's father: "Only Gujarati at home from now on, and no more sleepovers." Vaibhav's voice rose. Irfan noticed the father's hand tremble on the doorframe. At the hall, Vaibhav's father stood at the edge watching the elders dance garba, eyes wet. Later Irfan heard him say quietly, "I am afraid you will forget who we are." Vaibhav went silent, then said, "Papa, I'm not forgetting. Can we pick which things matter most?" His father breathed out. "Language at meals first." "And sleepovers with a phone call?" "Deal." Irfan watched two pairs of shoulders drop.

qa.q: Where was the Diwali party?
qa.a: The Diwali party was in the community hall in Leicester.

qa.q: What might Irfan have felt on seeing Vaibhav's father's hand tremble?
qa.a: Concern and sympathy, sensing that the strictness was tangled with worry.

qa.q: What turning point eased the argument?
qa.a: Vaibhav asking to pick which things matter most, so the father named language at meals and agreed to sleepovers with a phone call.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav's father have been feeling while watching the elders dance?
qa.a: Wistful and afraid of losing the culture, yet loving; the wet eyes show it.

grounding: A parent abroad tightens rules from love and fear of losing the culture, and dialogue about what matters softens the lines.

passage: On a Saturday afternoon in a Delhi flat, Vandana video-called her cousin Darshan in New Jersey. His screen shook as he carried the phone to the balcony. "Mummy has banned English at the dinner table," Darshan whispered, "and says no more dating unless she approves the family." Behind him Vandana heard his mother's voice, high and strained: "We left everything so you wouldn't lose it." Vandana saw Darshan roll his eyes, but she also saw the pinched shoulders as his mother wiped the counter over and over. "She sounds scared, not angry, no?" Vandana said. "Ask her what she is afraid of losing, and tell her what you can promise to keep." Darshan was quiet. "Hindi at dinner twice a week, calls to Nani on Sundays. I'll try tonight."

qa.q: Where was Darshan during the video call?
qa.a: Darshan was in New Jersey.

qa.q: Why does Vandana suggest asking a question instead of arguing, and what does Vandana want for Darshan?
qa.a: Vandana reads the mother as scared, not angry, judging by the strained voice and pinched shoulders, and wants Darshan and his mother to talk openly.

qa.q: What did Vandana suggest Darshan try?
qa.a: Ask what his mother is afraid of losing and offer promises to keep, such as Hindi at dinner twice a week and calls to Nani on Sundays.

qa.q: What might Darshan's mother have been feeling when she said We left everything?
qa.a: Fear and love mixed together, afraid the family's culture would be lost.

grounding: A parent abroad tightens rules on dating and language from fear of loss, and a relative suggests dialogue about what truly matters.

subtype: Not Indian enough or not local enough [Receiver]
passage:
Saturday. Home in Dharamshala for the holidays, Tenzin heard a cousin sigh, "You've gone so Western, you don't even eat properly." Tenzin laughed it off, but it stayed in the stomach.
Tuesday. Back in Dublin, a classmate said, "You'll never really be one of us, will you?" and turned back to the group chat. Tenzin walked out of the lecture hall feeling like an outsider wherever Tenzin stood.
Thursday. Tenzin told Usha over tea in the student centre. Usha listened, then said, "Both of them are using a tiny box. You're allowed to be all of it." Tenzin thought about that and answered, "I like momos and I like the rain here. I don't have to apologise for either." Usha raised her cup.

qa.q: Where was Tenzin on Tuesday?
qa.a: Tenzin was back in Dublin.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel after the classmate's remark, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hurt and unseen; Tenzin walked out of the lecture hall.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin move forward?
qa.a: Telling Usha, who called both labels a tiny box, and then claiming a blended identity without apology.

qa.q: What does Usha's reply show about how Usha sees the labels?
qa.a: That they come from narrow ideas, not from anything wrong with Tenzin.

grounding: A young adult is told they are too Western at home and too foreign abroad, and claims a blended identity without apology.

subtype: Not Indian enough or not local enough [Receiver]
passage: Hansa, come and sit. When I was twenty I studied in London, and people said I was too Indian to be one of them: my accent, my tiffin, the way I said thank you twice. Then I visited Kolkata in the holidays, and my aunts said I'd become too English, since I said sorry after every sentence and didn't know the bus number. I cried in my roommate Meg's room. Meg said, "You're the only person I know who is both. That's twice as much, not half." I carried that home like a stone in a pocket. On the next visit I made luchi and a cheese sandwich and put them on one plate. Nobody complained. Now I let both sides claim me, and I don't ask permission. Sonali

qa.q: Where did Sonali study at twenty?
qa.a: Sonali studied in London.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when the aunts said Sonali had become too English?
qa.a: Hurt and out of place; Sonali cried in Meg's room.

qa.q: What choice did Sonali make on the next visit?
qa.a: Sonali put luchi and a cheese sandwich on one plate, showing a blended identity without apology.

qa.q: How did Meg see Sonali?
qa.a: As someone with two worlds, twice as much rather than half of each.

grounding: A young adult told they are too foreign abroad and too English at home claims a blended identity without apology.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Thomas, listen. I came back to Bengaluru at twenty after five years in Perth, and I expected to slide right in. Instead the city had moved without me: the lane had a new flyover, my friends had new jokes and I didn't know the auto fare. Worse, I had changed too. The noise was too much and my Kannada slow. I felt like a guest in my own house. My mother said, "Give it time. You're not late." I began small: I took the bus with a route written on my hand, went to the same bakery every Saturday, and asked my old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending. After some months I noticed I'd stopped feeling out of step. Nobody handed me a place. I built one slowly. Anjali

qa.q: How many years had Anjali spent in Perth?
qa.a: Anjali spent five years in Perth.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel back in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Out of step, like a guest in the family house, since both the city and Anjali had changed.

qa.q: What choices helped Anjali, and why?
qa.a: Asking an old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending, and building small routines like the bakery, so belonging grew slowly.

qa.q: What did Anjali's mother mean by You're not late?
qa.a: That there was no deadline for fitting in, and patience with the place and oneself was enough.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience brings a new fit.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Nikita landed in Pune after six years in Toronto, and her suitcase did not. The airline said tomorrow. Outside, monsoon rain hammered the taxi rank, drivers shouted prices in Marathi that Nikita understood but answered slowly, and the phone was almost dead. Cousin Kalyani finally found Nikita under the shed. "You look lost," Kalyani said, laughing gently. Nikita's eyes stung. The city had rebuilt itself, and the road to the old school now had a metro pillar in the middle. Even Nikita's own jokes sounded odd in this air. "I don't know who I am here," Nikita said in the car. Kalyani answered, "You're the one who ate all the mango pickle, remember? Give it a week. You'll get the auto rates back." Nikita smiled at the windshield.

qa.q: What did the airline say about the suitcase?
qa.a: The airline said tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling in the car, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lost and out of step; Nikita's eyes stung and Nikita said not knowing who Nikita is here.

qa.q: What small step could help Nikita fit in again?
qa.a: Give it a week, relearn the auto rates and let familiar things like the mango pickle return.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Nikita?
qa.a: As a familiar cousin beneath the changes who needs time; Kalyani laughed gently and recalled the mango pickle.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience begins a new fit.

passage: Sunday, late. Sorting my two cultures like a cupboard tonight. Keeping: the Sunday dosa breakfast that Amma taught me, the phone call to Ajji on the first of every month, and saying thank you to the bus driver the way people here do. Letting go: the belief that I must always say yes to every relative's plan. Chetan from the flat above came for dosa and asked why I make the batter the night before. I explained and he grinned, then taught me to make his grandmother's chai from Nairobi. I'm thinking that one day I'll teach a child both, without saying this is the right way. Just: this is what our table looks like. Kiran

qa.q: What breakfast does Kiran keep on Sundays?
qa.a: Kiran keeps the Sunday dosa breakfast.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about the customs, and what shows it?
qa.a: Affection and calm ownership; Kiran carefully chooses what to keep and pictures a shared table.

qa.q: What could Kiran do next with these choices?
qa.a: Teach a child both, showing what the table looks like without presenting one way as right.

qa.q: What might Chetan have felt about sharing chai?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, since Chetan grinned and taught the recipe from a grandmother in Nairobi.

grounding: A young adult picks customs, foods and values to keep from each culture and plans to pass them on with warmth.

passage:
Nirmala: Onam's coming and I'm torn. Do I make the whole sadhya alone in a tiny London kitchen? 😅
Sangeeta: Why not just the parts you love? I skip the fifteen curries and make three.
Nirmala: True. The payasam has to stay. That's mine.
Sangeeta: And what do you drop?
Nirmala: The rule that I must cook while everyone else sits. My flatmates can chop.
Sangeeta: So you keep the food and change the rule 🙂
Nirmala: Exactly. And I'll play the old song Appa sends me every year. I want to teach it to my niece someday.
Sangeeta: Lovely. Save me a seat 🎉

qa.q: Which dish does Nirmala say has to stay?
qa.a: The payasam has to stay.

qa.q: How does Nirmala feel about deciding what to keep, and what shows it?
qa.a: Warm and confident; Nirmala names what is loved, keeps it and changes the rule about cooking alone.

qa.q: What rule does Nirmala change, and why?
qa.a: The rule that one person cooks while everyone else sits, since the flatmates can chop and the meal becomes shared.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta respond to the plan?
qa.a: Encouragingly, by summing it up and asking to save a seat.

grounding: A young adult chooses which customs and foods to keep and change and plans to pass them on with warmth.

passage: Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki, and Alka's plan for a Diwali dinner shrank to the five people who could walk. The electricity flickered once and died. Alka lit the diyas that were meant only as decoration and used them to see. Down the hall, Hrithik knocked with a bag of naan from the last open shop. Two friends from the language class arrived stamping snow off their boots, one carrying a pot of rice, the other a story about a grandmother's festival in Lagos. They ate by candlelight, in a mix of Hindi, English and one shared Finnish greeting. Alka looked at the messy table and realised nobody there shared the same ancestors, but they shared this evening, and for the first time in months the flat felt like home.

qa.q: What had stopped the trains in Helsinki?
qa.a: Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling at the messy table?
qa.a: Warm and at home, realising that belonging came from shared time, not shared ancestry.

qa.q: What made the evening work despite the storm?
qa.a: Adapting the plan to the five who could walk over and using the diyas for light.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt bringing naan through the snow?
qa.a: Glad to contribute and to belong, since Hrithik made the effort to reach the group.

grounding: A young adult far from home builds a chosen circle around a festival meal, showing belonging built through shared time.

passage: On the first Sunday of every month, Tenzin's small Mumbai flat filled with people far from home: Jasleen from Ludhiana, a colleague from Guwahati, two students from Kochi. Each brought something: Jasleen's parathas, Tenzin's momos, a pot of fish curry. Nobody was related, and nobody had to explain a pause before a word in a mother tongue. Jasleen taught a Punjabi phrase for eat more and everyone tried it. Last month, when Tenzin's grandmother was unwell in Gangtok and Tenzin sat silent, Jasleen simply refilled the tea and stayed until midnight. Nothing was said about it. The next month a small brass bell appeared on the shelf, brought by whoever felt like it.

qa.q: How often does the group meet?
qa.a: The group meets on the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while sitting silent, and how did Jasleen's action help?
qa.a: Worried and alone; Jasleen's staying and refilling the tea eased the loneliness.

qa.q: What makes this circle work?
qa.a: Shared time and small kindnesses, like a potluck and phrases from each language.

qa.q: Why might Jasleen have said nothing about staying until midnight?
qa.a: Because the kindness needed no words; staying was enough to show care.

grounding: A young adult far from home builds a circle of friends around shared meals, languages and kindness.

passage: I noticed Zubin at the ward office on a Tuesday, holding a form upside down. New in the city, Zubin was reading the Marathi headings with a finger, lips moving, while an old man behind kept sighing. I told myself to mind my own business, and then didn't. I said, "Sit here, I'll get you water," and asked, "Can I help with the form?" Zubin's shoulders dropped. We did it line by line, and I explained the address section and where to line up. Then I introduced Zubin to the clerk I know, and to Mrs. Rao at the tea stall: "This is Zubin, new in our lane." Weeks later Zubin greeted me by name in the market. It costs so little to offer a seat. Alka

qa.q: Where did Alka first see Zubin?
qa.a: Alka first saw Zubin at the ward office on a Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Alka tell Alka to mind Alka's own business and then not do it?
qa.a: Alka felt a pull of reluctance but also sympathy for Zubin's struggle, so chose to help.

qa.q: What small welcomes did Alka offer?
qa.a: A seat, water, help with the form and introductions to the clerk and Mrs. Rao.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt when Alka offered a seat?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone; the shoulders dropped.

grounding: A local sees a newcomer struggling with language and a form and offers a seat, help and introductions.

passage: Community centre supervisor's note, Rafiq. On Thursday I watched Sunaina, one of our volunteers, notice a new arrival standing at the counter with a form and a worried face. Sunaina put a chair beside the counter, offered tea and said, "Would it help if we did the form together?" They filled it in line by line. Sunaina then introduced the newcomer to two people in the reading room and wrote the centre's timings on a card. I did not step in. Later I asked Sunaina about it, and Sunaina shrugged: "I remember arriving somewhere new." The following week the newcomer came back and sat with the reading group.

qa.q: What did Sunaina write on a card?
qa.a: Sunaina wrote the centre's timings on a card.

qa.q: What do Sunaina's shrug and the words I remember arriving somewhere new suggest?
qa.a: Empathy from personal memory of being new, which is why Sunaina noticed the worried face.

qa.q: What made Sunaina's help work?
qa.a: Offering a chair and tea and doing the form together before introducing people, so the newcomer had support step by step.

qa.q: How might the newcomer have felt at the counter and later?
qa.a: Worried and unsure at first, then relieved and welcomed, which is why the newcomer came back the following week.

grounding: A local volunteer sees a new arrival struggling with a form and offers a seat, help and introductions.
